v001.objective: Open the batch's first lesson: name what Legal Support Help does, and that from today everything they do is a law firm's work product.
talk: Welcome the batch by name and say which lesson this is — Lesson 1, VA Essentials.
Two things carry through all 18 days: accuracy and confidentiality. Everything after this builds on them.
Housekeeping: cameras on for discussions, type 'done' in the GC at the end of every task, and all submissions go to their own Assessments/Activities folder.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day, everyone! Welcome to Day 1 of your Foundational Training. 😊

Kindly proceed right away to your first set of tasks for today's session. Thank you.

Topics: Common Terms Used & Auto Liability Insurance

Reminders for the whole training:
• Type "done" here in the GC after every task.
• Save every output in your own Assessments/Activities folder.
• Follow the file naming convention given for each task — the name is part of the grade.

keys: Tools they must have working today: Smart Advocate (SA) access, Nitro Pro (or another PDF editor that merges and edits text), Microsoft Word, Notepad.
SECURITY SOP: SA is on the 2nd password during training shifts and goes back to the 1st password at end of shift. VAs never change this password themselves.
pitfalls: Trainees who 'watch' with no notes — tell them now that the monitoring sheet items are graded.
Someone missing a tool. Settle it today, not on a demo day.

v002.objective: Set the bar: by the end they support a U.S. firm professionally — not just finish tasks.
talk: Read the objective, then put it in their words: structure, operations and expectations of U.S. law firms.
Point out what is coming: legal practice, firm types, areas of law, clientele, U.S. time zones and states, cultural context, the legal system, key terminology.
Say plainly that every item on that list shows up in a graded activity later.
pitfalls: Treating the objective slide as a formality. Ask one person to say it back before moving on.

v003.objective: Give them the map of the lesson so they can see where each part lands.
talk: Walk the agenda top to bottom, one line each — do not teach it here.
Flag the two items that become homework tonight: Common Terms and Auto Liability Insurance.
pitfalls: Teaching the agenda. It is a map; the parts come later.

v004.objective: Make cultural alignment concrete: U.S. legal culture, deadlines, confidentiality and tone are the job, not background.
talk: Professionalism, proactivity and cultural awareness are what get a VA kept on a firm.
Anticipating a need beats waiting to be told — that is the difference between hours renewed and a project ended.
Confidentiality is covered properly in Lesson 2, but it starts today.
pitfalls: Hearing 'cultural awareness' as accent training. It is deadlines, directness, and knowing what may not be said.

v020.objective: Place the Legal VA in the firm: a skilled remote professional, from admin through legal research.
talk: Why firms hire VAs: streamline operations, raise efficiency, keep attorney hours on legal work.
A Legal VA is not a generic VA — the work is file work on live cases.
pitfalls: Thinking 'virtual' means informal. The output is a law firm's work product either way.

v021.objective: Show the trade the firm is making: routine work moves to the VA so lawyers keep case preparation and client communication.
talk: Scheduling, email, documents — those are the routine tasks that come across.
Everything they take off the attorney's desk has to come back right the first time; a correction costs the firm more than the task saved.
pitfalls: Assuming routine means low stakes. A missed calendar entry is a missed deadline.

v022.objective: Benefits 1 and 2 — efficiency and cost — from the firm's side of the table.
talk: Efficiency: a skilled VA finishes faster and more accurately than an untrained in-house hire.
Cost: no benefits, no office space, no equipment for the firm.
Say the consequence: they are being paid for throughput and accuracy, and both are measured.

v023.objective: Benefits 3 and 4 — specialized skills and flexibility.
talk: Specialized skills: legal research, document preparation, transcription — this is why the 18 days exist.
Flexibility: VAs often cover outside traditional business hours, and U.S. time zones are the reason.
pitfalls: Hearing 'flexibility' as 'no fixed schedule'. Shifts are set; coverage is the point.

v024.objective: Benefit 5 — better client service, because attorneys get their time back.
talk: The client feels the VA's work even when the client never speaks to the VA.
Whether a VA may speak to clients at all is firm policy — that comes back in the Lesson 2 scenarios.

v025.objective: Open Tasks and Roles: firms run from one attorney to multi-state organizations, and handle nearly every kind of matter.
talk: Everything in this part answers one question for them: what will I actually be asked to do?
Tell them the five scenarios are coming and will be graded on reasoning, not on guessing the label.

v026.objective: Separate Legal Assistant from Paralegal cleanly.
talk: Both support the practice; the duties differ.
Our VAs work the Legal Assistant side of that line unless a firm says otherwise.
keys: Legal Assistant — administrative support: calendars, documents, file upkeep, financial and operational tasks.
Paralegal — substantive legal work delegated by an attorney: research, drafting pleadings, discovery; works under attorney supervision.
Neither may give legal advice. That line is absolute.
pitfalls: Using the titles interchangeably on a call with a client or a provider.

v027.objective: Make the Legal Assistant's day concrete, and note how close it sits to a legal secretary's.
talk: Appointments, document preparation, financial and operational tasks.
Ask the room which of those they have done in any job — most have done all of them, just not on a case file.

v028.objective: State the hinge of this part: the type of firm changes the job and the environment.
talk: Same title, different firm, different day. Keep this in mind for the scenarios.

v029.objective: Give the range — solo attorney up to multi-state, hundreds of staff.
talk: Size drives how specialized or how broad their work will be.

v030.objective: Tie task mix to firm type before naming the four categories.
talk: The kind of work follows the kind of firm. Nobody chooses their task mix; the firm's structure does.

v031.objective: Land the four task categories, then run the first two Practical Application scenarios against them.
talk: Transactional, Client-Centric, All-Around, Departmentalized — define each in one line.
Run Scenario 1 and Scenario 2 here. Make them justify the answer before you confirm it.

gc.label: Scenarios 1 and 2
gc.text:
PRACTICAL APPLICATION — Tasks and Roles
What type of Legal VA task category does each belong to? (Transactional / Client-Centric / All-Around / Departmentalized)

Scenario 1: A VA is asked to send a settlement breakdown today, and tomorrow to organize medical records.

Scenario 2: A VA works only in the medical records department, retrieving records daily.

Type your answer here with one sentence of reasoning. Thank you.

keys: Scenario 1 — Transactional Tasks. Different discrete task each day, no single owned function.
Scenario 2 — Departmentalized Tasks. One department, one repeated function, daily.
Transactional = task-by-task. Client-Centric = owns the client relationship. All-Around = everything, usually solo/small. Departmentalized = one function inside a larger firm.
pitfalls: Calling Scenario 1 'All-Around' — All-Around is about breadth of role in a small firm, not a different task each day.
Answering with the label alone. The reasoning is what is graded.

match: Scenario 1: "Transactional"
Scenario 2: "Departmentalized"
reasoning mentions varied/different tasks per day (S1)
reasoning mentions one department / single repeated function (S2)
nlp: Accept semantic equivalents: 'task-based', 'per-task', 'one-off tasks' for Transactional; 'specialized to one unit', 'records department only' for Departmentalized.
Score label and reasoning separately — a right label with absent or wrong reasoning caps at 50% for that scenario.
Reject answers that name two categories without choosing one.

rubric: Answered in own words, not read from the slide
Spoke up without being called on
trainer.feedback: What their reasoning showed about how they read a task list…

v032.objective: Smaller firms need multi-skilled VAs — that is how hours get built.
talk: In a small firm there is little to delegate, so range is what earns hours.
This is the setup for Scenario 3; do not give that answer away yet.

v033.objective: Name the consequence honestly — a VA judged unskilled loses hours or the project — then run Scenario 3.
talk: Say it straight: the firm's alternative is to work alone. Hours are not guaranteed.
Run Scenario 3 on the solo attorney practice.

gc.label: Scenario 3
gc.text:
PRACTICAL APPLICATION — Scenario 3
You are assigned to a solo attorney practice. The attorney asks you to answer calls, organize files, schedule appointments, and send billing follow-ups.

Question: What does this tell you about the type of law firm and your expected role?

Type your answer here. Thank you.

keys: Scenario 3 — a Small Law Firm or Solo Practice, and an All-Around role: one VA covering reception, files, calendar and billing follow-up.
Strong answers also say why: there is no department to hand work to.
pitfalls: Naming only the role or only the firm type. The question asks for both.

match: "Solo" or "Solo Practice" or "Small Law Firm"
"All-Around" role
at least two of: calls, files, scheduling, billing
nlp: Accept 'one-person firm', 'single attorney' for Solo; 'generalist', 'wears many hats' for All-Around.
Require both the firm type and the role for full marks.

rubric: Connected it to their own expected workload
trainer.feedback: Notes on how they read the firm from the task list…

v034.objective: Large firms move people between roles; comfort with that transfer is the requirement.
talk: A transfer out of intake into medical records is normal, not a demotion.
Setup for Scenario 4 — restructuring.

v035.objective: Close Tasks and Roles with the flexibility point, then run Scenarios 4 and 5.
talk: When a firm struggles, it keeps the VAs who have handled more than one role.
Run Scenario 4 (restructuring) and Scenario 5 (client communication restriction) back to back — they both come down to adapting to the firm's SOP.

gc.label: Scenarios 4 and 5
gc.text:
PRACTICAL APPLICATION — Scenarios 4 and 5

Scenario 4: You were originally assigned to the intake department, but the law firm later transferred you to medical records because another department needed support.
Question: Why does this happen, and what quality is the firm looking for?

Scenario 5: At one law firm, VAs are not allowed to communicate directly with clients, but at another firm they are allowed to follow up with clients regarding documents.
Question: What lesson should a Legal VA learn from this?

Type your answers here. Thank you.

keys: Scenario 4 — larger firms restructure departments by workload and staffing. Qualities sought: high flexibility, strong adaptability, proactive willingness to learn new tasks.
Scenario 5 — every firm has different policies and workflows. Adapt to the client's SOP, follow their rules, never assume procedures are the same across firms.
SOP ADHERENCE is the takeaway of this whole part: the firm's rule wins over what we were taught elsewhere.
pitfalls: Reading Scenario 4 as unfair treatment.
Answering Scenario 5 with 'both are fine' — the lesson is to follow the SOP of the firm you are on, and to verify before acting.

match: S4: "restructure" / workload / staffing needs
S4: "flexibility" AND "adaptability"
S5: "SOP"
S5: 'never assume' / policies differ per firm
nlp: Accept 'reorganize', 'reassign', 'department needs' for restructuring; 'willing to learn' counts toward adaptability.
S5 full marks require both: policies differ by firm AND the VA follows the client's SOP.
Flag any answer that says a VA may decide for themselves whether to contact a client — that is a hard fail on this item.

rubric: Asked what to do when an SOP is unclear
trainer.feedback: Notes on their attitude to reassignment and to firm rules…

v036.objective: Solo firms: one lawyer, often outside paralegals, personal attention, one or two focus areas.
talk: Solo practitioners may be new or very experienced — do not assume either.
For a VA: broadest role, closest contact with the attorney, least backup.
keys: Solo = 1 attorney. May hire outside paralegals and experts. General or specialized. VA role: All-Around.

v037.objective: Small / boutique firms: 2–10 attorneys, close collaboration, limited resources.
talk: Boutique means highly specialized and personalized, not small-time.
Limited resources mean more administrative load on the lawyers — which is exactly where the VA is used.
keys: Small/boutique = 2–10 attorneys. Autonomy, broad legal topics, resource constraints. VA role: All-Around to Transactional.

v038.objective: Medium firms: 50 to several hundred attorneys, partner-level service with real staffing behind it.
talk: Less prestige than large, more autonomy and a more strategic case load.
For a VA: departments start to exist, so work narrows.
keys: Medium = 50–several hundred attorneys. VA role: Departmentalized or Client-Centric.

v039.objective: Large firms: hundreds to thousands of attorneys, offices nationwide and abroad, fast and complex work.
talk: The largest U.S. firms run upward of 3,000 attorneys.
For a VA: narrow function, high volume, strict process — and transfers between departments, as in Scenario 4.
keys: Large = several hundred to thousands of attorneys, multi-office, multi-state and international. VA role: strictly Departmentalized.
pitfalls: Assuming large firms mean more interesting work. It usually means one slice of the process, done exactly to SOP.

v134.objective: Tips 1 and 2 — own the case management system, and account for time like a lawyer.
talk: Master the CMS: shortcuts, tagging, pulling reports and tasks. Self-sufficiency is the value.
Think like a lawyer: time is the firm's product. Log entries clearly and specifically.
keys: Our CMS in training is Smart Advocate (SA). From Lesson/Day 9 onward every demo is scored inside SA.
A good time entry names the system, the party and the task: 'Updated Clio with billing from OrthoSouth — 15 mins'.
pitfalls: Vague time entries ('worked on case'). They are unbillable and they get noticed.

v135.objective: Tips 3 and 4 — be proactive, and keep written communication clean.
talk: Proactive means anticipating the next step: the IME is scheduled, so offer the transport request.
Clear subject lines and bullet points. 'RECORDS REQUEST: OrthoSouth — Smith, John' tells the reader everything before they open it.
keys: Subject-line pattern used throughout this training: [Client Name] - [Entity] - [Type of Request].
pitfalls: Proactive is not acting outside authority. Offer, then wait for the go-ahead.

v136.objective: Tips 5 and 6 — know the PI process, and keep learning past the task list.
talk: The phases: intake → treatment → demand → negotiation → settlement. This is the spine of the whole program.
Tell them this exact lifecycle is the first Process Question on Reception day, and they will be asked what a VA does at each stage.
keys: PI case lifecycle: Intake → Treatment → Demand → Negotiation → Settlement.
Roles against the phases: Reception and Intake at the front, Claims and Provider Communication through treatment, Lien Negotiator after settlement.
pitfalls: Memorizing the five words without the VA tasks attached to each.

v137.objective: The mindset page — read it as a standard, not a poster.
talk: Precision, purpose, professionalism. Anticipate, act, lead quietly.
Close on the one that is graded every day: bring clarity, calm and confidence to every case you touch.
pitfalls: Rushing past it. This is the page to come back to when a trainee's attitude slips in week two.

v138.objective: Close the lesson and set tonight's homework: both assessments, plus monitoring items #5–7.
talk: Confirm both videos are watched and both reference files are open.
Give the homework, the folder and the deadline in one message, then take questions.
While they wait for their teammates, point them at the supplementary Personal Injury articles.

gc.text:

gc.text:

keys: Answer keys are in the trainer's Day 1 folder: the Common Terms Assessment key and the Auto Liability Insurance Assessment key. Check both tomorrow morning, with clarification and enrichment.

Tonight's homework also includes the Softphone instructional video (ONE sample type only) and the PPT review — Documents & Spreadsheets, Keyboard Shortcuts, Shadowing Etiquette — with monitoring items #8–9.
pitfalls: Submissions landing loose in the training folder instead of Assessments/Activities.
Watching the whole softphone video instead of one sample type, and running out of time.

grade.deliverable: Day 1 Homework — Common Terms & Auto Liability Insurance Assessments
grade.file: Common Terms and Auto Liability assessments, uploaded in Assessments/Activities

match: Both documents submitted in Assessments/Activities
Common Terms: exact term-to-definition matches against the answer key
Auto Liability: policy limit stated as per-person / per-accident (e.g. 25/50/25)
Auto Liability: coverage types named — BI, PD, UM, UIM, Med Pay/PIP, Collision, Comprehensive
nlp: Semantic similarity against the answer key per item, not string equality — accept a correct definition in the trainee's own words.
Normalize abbreviations both ways: BI/Bodily Injury, PD/Property Damage, UM/Uninsured Motorist, UIM/Underinsured Motorist, DOL/Date of Loss, LOR/Letter of Representation.
Mark an item wrong, not partial, where a coverage is defined as another coverage (UM described as UIM).

rubric: Answers in own words rather than copied
trainer.feedback: Which terms or coverages to re-teach for this trainee…

v001.objective: Open Law Firm Communication: every call a VA takes or makes is the firm speaking.
talk: Frame the day: softphones, call handling, and who we are allowed to say what to.
Tell them the afternoon is a breakout — Process Questions and the escalation exercise — so they listen for the answers now.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting our classroom discussion on Law Firm Communication.

Topics: Softphones · Call Handling · Law Firm Call Management · Attorney-Client Privilege

This afternoon (1:00–3:00 PM) we go into breakout for the Process Questions and the Escalation Handling exercise. Please take notes as we go — the answers come from this discussion. Thank you.

pitfalls: Trainees treating this as a soft topic. It is the one lesson where a mistake is a legal exposure, not a rework.

v004.objective: Name the first half: inbound calls — calls that come to the firm.
talk: Inbound is reception's world: whoever picks up decides what happens to that caller.
Tell them the ten inbound habits are each one page, and the first five decide whether the caller stays.

v005.objective: Separate the three inbound roles so they know which hat they are wearing.
talk: Receptionist, Intake Specialist, Appointment Setter — one caller can pass through all three.
Our program trains all three: Reception on Days 3–4, Intake from Day 7, Calendaring on Days 5–6.
keys: Receptionist — greets, screens, triages, transfers, documents.
Intake Specialist — qualifies the lead, asks the intake questions, collects the documents.
Appointment Setter — confirms availability and plots the attorney's calendar.

v006.objective: Show what reception intake really decides: whether this is a good lead.
talk: Determining a good lead is a judgement made in the first minute, on the intake questions.
A bad screen costs the attorney a consultation slot; a missed good lead costs the firm a case.
pitfalls: Screening by how upset the caller is rather than by the facts of the matter.

v010.objective: Tone is the first impression — and it is role-specific. Start building the tone matrix here.
talk: Callers can hear a smile; they can also hear impatience. Calm and clarity are the default.
Start the tone matrix now and finish it on the court/adjuster/opposing-counsel pages: the tone changes with who is on the line, the facts never do.
keys: TONE MATRIX (used in the Process Questions and the Day 4 mock calls):
Worried client — warm, patient, reassuring; no promises about outcome or value.
Insurance adjuster — neutral, brief, factual; share only what is allowed.
Court staff — formal, precise, deferential; case number and case style ready.
Opposing counsel — correct and minimal; never volunteer anything.
Medical provider — professional and cooperative; public information only.
pitfalls: One tone for everyone. A client tone with an adjuster leaks; an adjuster tone with a client sounds cold.

v011.objective: Script plus tone is what makes a hard call (past-due invoices) survivable.
talk: The script carries compliance; the tone carries the relationship. They need both.
This is Process Question 4 — scripted versus freeform. Let them hear the answer forming here.
keys: Scripted calls win on professionalism and compliance: nothing is improvised that could mislead or disclose.
Freeform wins on rapport — so the answer is a script as the floor, with the VA's own words on top, never instead.

v022.objective: Documentation is part of the call, not paperwork after it.
talk: Document to the firm's preferred method: email, call log, CRM note.
If it is not in the CMS, it did not happen. From Day 9 they do this in Smart Advocate for real.
keys: Every note names: who called, what they wanted, what was said, what happens next, and who owns the next step.
pitfalls: Writing notes from memory at the end of the shift.
Notes that record the VA's opinion of the caller rather than the facts.

v037.objective: Provider calls: public information only — and this is where the privilege line gets tested.
talk: Name, phone number, address: public. Anything else, stop.
Some providers will ask for private information. The answer is that we will send it through the authorized request, not read it out.
keys: Confidential information — anything we learn about the client's matter; protected by duty.
Privileged communication — communication between client and attorney for legal advice; protected from disclosure altogether.
This distinction is Process Question 3, and it is the one trainees most often get wrong.
pitfalls: Reading out a date of birth or SSN because the person on the line sounds official.

v040.objective: Adjuster calls: the guardrails, before anyone practises one.
talk: Put the two lists on the board before the script. They matter more than the wording.
This is the same rule they will use on Day 10 when opening claims.
keys: DO NOT SHARE with an adjuster: Date of Birth, Email address, SSN, VIN.
MAY SHARE: client's first and last name (no middle name), vehicle information such as the plate number, city and state only, and the law firm's phone number.
Why it is safe: those items are already in the police report the adjuster has.
pitfalls: Giving the client's own phone number instead of the firm's.
Confirming a detail the adjuster reads out — confirming is disclosing.

v045.objective: Court calls: formal, prepared, and never substantive.
talk: Confirm the department first, then give the case number and case style.
Court staff are not a source of advice and we do not argue the matter with them.
keys: Have ready before dialling: case number, case style, attorney's name, the specific ask.
pitfalls: Calling the court without the case number in front of them.

v048.objective: Opposing counsel: correct, minimal, and nothing volunteered.
talk: Identify the firm, make the single request, confirm what was agreed, end the call.
Never discuss the facts, the treatment, the demand or the client's situation — not even to be helpful.
keys: A voicemail to opposing counsel carries name, firm, callback number and the subject only — never case details.
pitfalls: Being drawn into small talk about the case. That is the most common real-world leak.

grade.deliverable: Entity communication matrix — who may be told what

match: Adjuster: DOB, email, SSN, VIN listed as never shared
Adjuster: name, plate, city/state, firm phone listed as shareable
Provider: public information only
Opposing counsel: no case details, no volunteered information
Court: case number and case style
nlp: Score per entity; a correct rule for one entity does not carry to another.
Treat 'I would check with the attorney first' as a correct answer where the item is not on the allowed list.
Any answer that permits sharing SSN, DOB, email or VIN with an adjuster is a hard fail regardless of composite score.

rubric: Professional deference — defers to attorney rather than guessing
Holds the line politely under pressure
Phone etiquette: identifies firm, confirms, closes
trainer.feedback: How they held the line when the caller pushed…

v053.objective: Close outbound with the preparation habit: name, number, purpose and documents before dialling.
talk: Prepared calls are short calls. Unprepared calls are the ones that need a second call.
Double-check everything, and have the note half-written before the phone rings.

v024.objective: Name the second half: outbound — the firm reaching out, where who we are calling changes everything.
talk: Five audiences: clients, invoices, providers, adjusters, court and opposing counsel.
Each has its own script and its own limit on what may be said.

v054.objective: Close the deck, then run the breakout: handouts, Process Questions, the escalation exercise, and tonight's homework.
talk: Post the four handouts, then split the group.
Run the five Priority questions if time is short; the full eleven if the batch is moving well.
Finish with the Escalation Handling exercise, then give the homework.

gc.label: Process Questions — Priority track (5)
gc.text:
PROCESS QUESTIONS

1. Evaluate the pros and cons of using softphones in high-confidentiality legal settings. What security risks must be considered?
2. Judge whether scripted calls are more effective than freeform conversations in maintaining professionalism and compliance.
3. Break down the difference between confidential information and privileged communication. Why is this distinction important?
4. Compare the communication protocols and tone required when interacting with clients vs. defense counsel or court staff.
5. Evaluate the risks of providing incomplete or incorrect information to each type of entity. Which scenario could be most legally damaging?

Save your answers in your Assessments/Activities folder using this file name:
Law_Firm_Communications_Training_Process_Question_Answers_[your first name]

Type "done" here once uploaded. Thank you.

gc.label: Homework — softphones and the PPTs
gc.text:
📌 To be accomplished outside training hours. 📌

Topic: Softphones
Task 1 – Watch the instructional video on Softphones. Watch ONE SAMPLE TYPE only for your takeaways on your monitoring sheet; you may continue during idle time.
https://drive.google.com/file/d/15aa9GSp3DtOFCG2nQD4CgDPsljA1usQ2/view

Topic: Documents & Spreadsheets, Keyboard Shortcuts, and Shadowing Etiquette
Task 2 – Review the following PPT materials, slide by slide.
2026 VERSION: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1-uB07Lu7nPeRpdDwOzvAKFMjZbXKQW-r
OLD VERSION: https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1sR8tjpMXPGWJo9cldpNWFdPhtMgq4n-y

Task 3 – Update items #8–9 in your monitoring sheet. Thank you.

keys: Full list is 11 questions; the Priority track is the 5 above. Use the Priority track when time is short.
Naming convention: Law_Firm_Communications_Training_Process_Question_Answers_[VA's first name]. The file name is graded.
Escalation Handling exercise runs after the questions — Canva deck in the trainer's Day 1 folder.

Answer anchors: softphone risk = unsecured wifi, shared devices, call recording and overheard audio at home; privilege vs confidentiality = all privileged communication is confidential, not all confidential information is privileged; most legally damaging = wrong or partial information to opposing counsel or an adjuster, because it can be used against the client.
pitfalls: Answers copied from the handout wording instead of reasoned out.
Wrong file name, or saved outside Assessments/Activities — both lose marks before the content is read.
Running out of time and skipping the escalation exercise. Cut questions, not the exercise.

grade.deliverable: Process Questions — Law Firm Communication (Priority track, 5 questions)

match: File name matches the convention exactly, with the trainee's first name
File is in Assessments/Activities
Q1: names at least two security risks (unsecured network, shared/home device, recording, overheard audio)
Q2: takes a position AND names compliance or professionalism as the reason
Q3: states that privileged communication is attorney-client communication for legal advice, and is a subset of confidential information
Q4: tone differs by entity — warm/reassuring for client, formal/minimal for court and defense counsel
Q5: names an entity and why the harm is worst there
nlp: Semantic scoring per question against the answer anchors, not keyword counting; five questions, equal weight.
Q3 is the discriminator: an answer that treats the two terms as synonyms scores zero on that item however well written.
Reward a position plus a reason on Q2 and Q5; an answer that only restates the question scores 25% of the item.

trainer.feedback: Which of the five to re-teach before the Day 3 reception work…

v001.objective: Open the PI Workflow deck: the one map the rest of the 18 days hangs on.
talk: Tell them plainly: every role they will train for sits somewhere on this map.
By the end of this deck they must be able to name the stages in order, unprompted.

gc.label: Open the session
gc.text:
Good day! We are starting our classroom discussion on the Personal Injury Workflow.

By the end of this part you should be able to name the stages of a PI case in order, and say what a Legal VA does at each one. Please take notes — this is the first Process Question. Thank you.

pitfalls: Trainees who know PI from another firm and assume the stages are named the same. Use our stage names.

v002.objective: Set the frame: every claim turns on its own facts, and PI law decides who can be claimed against.
talk: No two claims are identical — which is why SOP matters more than memory.
PI law governs what creates grounds for a claim and who the claim can be made against.

v003.objective: The stage list — have them write it down before anything is explained.
talk: Read the stages in order, then have the room say them back without the slide.
Mark where each specialist role lives: Reception and Intake at the front, Claims at set-up, Provider Communication through treatment and records, Lien Negotiator after settlement.
keys: Legal Intake and Consultation → Claims Set-Up and Liability Determination → Treatment → Collecting Medical Bills and Records → Demand → Negotiation → Settlement and Disbursement (→ Litigation where no settlement is reached).
The short form used elsewhere in this program: Intake → Treatment → Demand → Negotiation → Settlement.
pitfalls: Putting Demand before records are collected. The package cannot be built without the bills and records.

grade.deliverable: PI lifecycle, in order, with the VA's task at each stage

match: All stages present and in order
Intake: documents collected, lead qualified
Claims set-up: claims opened, LOR sent, policy limits requested
Treatment: records and bills requested, lien tracking
Demand: package assembled
Negotiation and settlement: releases, net sheet, disbursement
nlp: Accept the short five-stage form as complete if each stage carries a VA task.
Order errors are scored separately from missing stages: a complete list in the wrong order caps at 60%.
An answer that lists stages with no VA task attached scores half — the question asks what the VA does.

trainer.feedback: Which stage they could not place…

v004.objective: Legal Intake: converting a contact into a client is the firm's most important process.
talk: This is where the case is won or lost before anyone looks at the law.
The information collected here is what every later stage runs on — Day 7 and Day 8 are entirely about it.
keys: Intake collects: client details, date of loss, how it happened, injuries, treatment so far, insurance on both sides, the police report.
pitfalls: Thinking intake is clerical. It is the firm's sales and evidence function at once.

v005.objective: The consultation: what the attorney covers with the client, and where the VA's limit is.
talk: The attorney discusses circumstances and concerns, and sets expectations.
The VA prepares, schedules and documents — the VA never advises on the merits or the value.
pitfalls: Answering a client's 'how much is my case worth'. That is the attorney's, always.

v006.objective: Investigation and how the firm gets paid: the contingency fee.
talk: Most PI lawyers work on contingency — a share of the settlement, nothing if the case loses, though costs may still apply.
Contrast with a retainer, which is paid up front. This exact comparison is a Day 7 Process Question.
keys: Contingency fee — a percentage of the recovery, charged only on a win; the client fronts no legal fee.
Retainer — paid up front and drawn down; typical of transactional and non-PI matters.
Effect on onboarding: contingency lowers the barrier to signing, so screening at intake does the filtering a fee would otherwise do.

v007.objective: Opening claims: contacting the insurer is one of the first steps, and it is the Claims Specialist's job.
talk: Insurers drive the pace of the whole case, especially in auto claims.
Days 10 to 12 are this one page in full: opening claims, LORs, and the SA workflow.

v008.objective: Claims set-up and liability: secure the documents, then identify every party at fault.
talk: Every possible at-fault party gets a claim opened with their insurer. Missing one loses coverage.
This is where UM/UIM gets opened — and failing to open it in time is a Day 10 Process Question.
keys: 1P = our client's own insurer. 3P = the at-fault party's insurer. Both get an LOR.
UM/UIM is opened against our client's own policy where the at-fault party has no or too little coverage. Late opening can forfeit the claim under the policy's notice terms.
pitfalls: Assuming one defendant means one claim. Multiple liable parties means multiple claims.

v009.objective: Policy limits and coverages: request the Dec Pages and read them.
talk: The firm requests the policy information for both plaintiff and defendant, then reads the declarations page.
The limit decides what the case can recover — this is the Day 11 Policy Disclosure activity.
keys: On a Dec Page, find: named insured, policy period, BI limits (per person / per accident), PD, UM/UIM, Med Pay or PIP, and any deductible.
A limit written 25/50/25 means $25,000 per person BI / $50,000 per accident BI / $25,000 PD.
pitfalls: Reading the per-accident figure as the per-person figure. It overstates the case by double or more.

v010.objective: Treatment begins: the client must treat promptly, and the records become the evidence.
talk: Treatment both heals the client and documents the injury — gaps in treatment are read as gaps in injury.
The Client Communication Specialist keeps that contact going.
pitfalls: Letting a client go quiet during treatment. A treatment gap is the single most common weakness in a claim.

v011.objective: What the client should keep while treating: providers seen, out-of-pocket costs, missed work.
talk: Those three feed the damages side of the demand. A VA who prompts for them early saves weeks later.

v012.objective: Collecting bills and records: when requests start, and why timing matters.
talk: Requests begin roughly 4–8 weeks after the date of loss, and in earnest as soon as treatment is complete.
Days 13 to 17 are this stage: MedLOR, bills and records, lien balance verification.
keys: Request sequence: MedLOR with the signed HIPAA authorization → bills and records → lien balance verification → the demand package.
pitfalls: Requesting records before the HIPAA authorization is valid and signed. The provider will refuse and the week is lost.

v013.objective: The firm coordinates with providers: all charges accounted for, treatment plan followed.
talk: Chasing a provider is normal work, not an exception — the Day 15 upskill covers assertive follow-ups.
Every charge must be accounted for before a demand goes out, or the demand understates the case.

v014.objective: The demand package: what it is and what it has to prove.
talk: It sets out the case, the injuries and the compensation sought, with the records behind it.
The goal is to make the adjuster's decision easy and well evidenced.
keys: A demand package carries: the demand letter, liability evidence (police report, photos), medical records and bills, wage loss proof, and the lien or LOP information.

v015.objective: What goes in the letter once everything is gathered.
talk: Medical bills, police report, evidence of fault — then the demand itself.
Each document in the package does a job: this is the Day 13 'Document Detectives' exercise.

v016.objective: The insurer reviews, then negotiation starts.
talk: The firm negotiates toward a satisfactory settlement; the first offer is rarely the last.
Packages can be submitted by mail, email or e-portal depending on the carrier.

v017.objective: Settlement: a voluntary agreement that ends the dispute.
talk: It speeds up resolution and removes the risk of trial for both sides.
Settlement is where the Lien Negotiator's work begins, not ends — Days 17 and 18.

v018.objective: Negotiations: the client is told immediately and the options are discussed.
talk: The firm notifies the client as soon as an offer arrives. Delay here is an ethics problem, not a scheduling one.
The options come from the attorney's experience; the VA documents and schedules.
pitfalls: A VA characterising an offer as good or bad to the client. Report it, do not evaluate it.

v019.objective: Disbursement: the settlement agreement, the deductions and what reaches the client.
talk: Reductions, liens, costs and fees come off before the client's net.
The net sheet and the closing statement must match to the cent — that is a Day 18 rule and a graded one.
keys: Order of operations: gross settlement → attorney's fee → case costs → medical liens and LOPs (after reduction) → net to client.
The net to client on the net sheet must equal the closing statement exactly.

v020.objective: Litigation: what happens when the insurer will not value the injuries properly.
talk: Most claims settle; a suit is filed when they do not.
Once suit is filed, deadlines become court deadlines — which is why calendaring is its own lesson.

v021.objective: Reception: the first point of contact, facing every kind of caller.
talk: Adjusters, opposing counsel, provider staff, courts and anxious clients all come through one line.
Tie it back to the tone matrix from Law Firm Communication, then forward to the Day 3–4 reception work.
keys: Reception's four jobs on every call: identify the caller, screen, triage, and document before transferring.

v022.objective: Calendar management: missed deadlines can dismiss a case or forfeit a right.
talk: Say the consequence out loud — dismissal, forfeiture. This is why Days 5 and 6 are strict.
Preview the rules they will be scored on: EST visible, 15-minute buffers, consult days and cut-offs.
keys: Standing calendar rules: everything in EST, 15-minute buffer before and after, email reminder one day prior, event titled [Meeting Type] – [Client Name].

v023.objective: Appointment Setter: keeps the client pipeline and the attorney's day working.
talk: Mandatory data on every setting call: name, callback number, DOB, DOL. No exceptions.
keys: Collect on every call: client name, callback number, Date of Birth, Date of Loss.

v024.objective: Scheduler: organized scheduling is what lets attorneys meet clients and hit tasks on time.
talk: Close the role list here, then move to the afternoon's work.

v025.objective: Close the deck, then run the afternoon: Process Questions, the confidentiality exercise, the call-listening set and Oscar's data-extraction activity.
talk: Post the sample recordings, then set the Process Questions.
Run the Confidentiality & Call Response exercise after the questions.
Finish with the reception activity on VA Oscar's recordings — five data points — then give the CRM/CMS homework.

keys: This lesson's Process Questions (the PI Workflow set) are on the trainee's Process Questions page; the Receptionist Training set belongs to Lesson 4. Each has its own answer sheet and file name.
PI Workflow answer sheet: PI_Workflow_Process_Question_Answers_[VA's first name], saved in Assessments/Activities.
Priority track when time is short: the lifecycle with VA tasks, the effect of missing documentation, and the cost of a disorganized intake.

Answer anchor — missing documentation: without the police report liability is contested; without records the damages cannot be proven, so the demand is understated or delayed and the claim's value drops.

Answer anchor — disorganized intake: duplicated work, missed deadlines including the UM/UIM notice, lost evidence, and a client who loses confidence; the financial consequence is a lower settlement or a dropped case.
pitfalls: Listening to the recordings without the activity sheet open, then going back to re-listen.
Extracting fewer than five data points, or extracting them from Carlos's supplementary recordings instead of Oscar's.
Working on a local copy instead of the uploaded document in their own folder.

grade.deliverable: Reception activity — 5 data points from VA Oscar's recordings
grade.file: Completed activity sheet, uploaded in the trainee's own folder and finalized there

match: Exactly 5 data points extracted
Caller name as spoken on the recording
Callback number, digit for digit
Date of Loss in mm/dd/yyyy
Nature of the call / reason as stated
Action taken or transfer destination
nlp: Match names by phonetic and fuzzy similarity against the recording's transcript, not exact spelling — flag a near-miss for the facilitator rather than failing it.
Numbers are exact-match only: one wrong digit in a callback number or a DOL is wrong, not partial.
Accept any order of the five fields; score each field independently.

rubric: Worked from the uploaded sheet in their own folder
Asked before guessing an unclear field
trainer.feedback: Which field they lost and whether it was hearing or recording it…
